To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
constitutive activity of a GPCR can be caused by two distinct mechanisms that act in concert to determine ligand function.

1) constitutively active mutants of the CCK-2 receptor can be subdivided into two groups, 2) the first group of mutants is characterized by an increase in the efficacy of most ligands, and 3) the second group of mutants is defined by a combination of two factors that are independent of each other, i.e., an increase in efficacy for some but not all ligands and a decrease in the efficacy of other ligands.

the efficacy of partial agonists at constitutively signaling GPCRs is determined by two distinct yet mutually interacting mechanisms: 1) the ability of the agonist to shift the receptor equilibrium between the inactive and active conformational states, and 2) the ability of agonist to induce a conformational change in the receptor that is compatible with the activation of downstream signaling.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the functional consequences of activating mutations in GPCR ligand-binding pockets and provides evidence that ligand function at constitutive mutants is affected by distinct yet interacting mechanisms.
a previously unexplored aspect of GPCR activation and provides a new perspective on the relationship between receptor structure, constitutive activity, and ligand efficacy.
understanding the molecular mechanisms of GPCR activation and provides a basis for future development of novel therapeutics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ligand function at constitutive receptor mutants is affected in a complex manner by two interacting mechanisms, which are not mutually exclusive.
ligand activity at constitutively activated receptors is determined by the combined action of two independent yet interacting factors.
constitutive activity is a continuum rather than an "all or nothing" state.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ligands with different intrinsic activities can be discriminated by the same receptor, provided that it is in a different conformational state.

the constitutive activity of a GPCR is defined by the ability of an activating mutation to increase the efficacy of all ligands, whereas constitutively active receptors with altered ligand function should be classified as "mutant receptors with altered ligands."
ligand function at constitutive active receptor mutants is determined by two distinct yet interactive mechanisms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ligand activity at GPCR mutants is determined by a multiplicity of factors that are not necessarily related to the degree of basal activity.
the effects of activating mutations on ligand efficacy are determined by the interplay of two distinct yet interacting molecular mechanisms.

the functional consequences of activating mutations in GPCRs are not always predictable and that the use of a single constitutively active mutant to study the mechanism of action of a particular ligand may be misleading.
